newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels start freeing some hostages in Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rebels start freeing some hostages in Peru crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels started freeing on Sunday night what they said would be 225 of the roughly 340 hostages they held at the besieged Japanese embassy residence for more than five days.
The hostages started filing out of the front entrance of the embassy just before 10 p.m. local time (0300 GMT Monday) under the gaze of Red Cross officials.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas said in a statement read prior to the mass release that they were liberating prisoners who were not connected to the government as a Christmas gesture of good faith.

But they warned the government they would not release its men from the besieged residence unless President Alberto Fujimori agreed to their demand of setting free more than 400 jailed MRTA members -- something the government has already flatly rejected.
"We clarify and insist that the liberation of the authorities who are today prisoner will only be possible if the government sets free (our) comrades," the MRTA statement said.

It was read to crowds of waiting reporters by former labour minister Sandro Fuentes, who was released from the building to make the statement along with the Panamanian ambassador, the Spanish charge d'affaires and a U.N. official.
"We are proceeding to free people who are not connected to the policy of the regime directly or indirectly as a Christmas gesture," the rebel statement said.
But it also warned the government that "if Mr. Fujimori decides a military solution he will always find a Tupac Amaru (guerrilla)."
The sudden and dramatic mass release came as a surprise on Sunday night because there was no sign of any progress in negotiations.

Conditions inside the grand embassy residence were deteriorating fast, raising fears of health problems among the hostages. The government cut off running water, electricity and phone service early in the siege to put pressure on the rebels.
Just after the siege began its sixth day, several large buses drove up outside the residence.
Top government negotiator Domingo Palermo made his first appearance at the scene and chief Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig also stood by.

After almost an hour of extreme tension and conflicting rumours, the hostages began filing out of the entrance, most still wearing the clothing they donned for the reception last Tuesday at which they were captured.
Some shook hands with Red Cross officials waiting outside the door, apparently checking them off on a list of names.
Peruvian media reported the release with joy, mingled with regret that a final end to the crisis appeared not yet to have come.
Smiling and waving, the hostages were driven away in large buses from the scene of the residence.

Police sources and witnesses said they would be taken to a police hospital for checks. There were unconfirmed local media reports that Fujimori himself would greet the released hostages at the hospital.
